cards.heading: supply and borrow
cards.body: DeFi lending works as a peer-to-pool system. Suppliers deposit assets into a smart contract pool and earn interest. Borrowers take assets from the pool by posting collateral and paying interest. Everything is automated — no loan officer, no paperwork.

cards.heading: how interest rates work
cards.body: Rates are set algorithmically by supply and demand. When many people borrow (high utilization), interest rises — incentivizing more suppliers to deposit. When utilization drops, rates fall. Aave and Compound use rate curves with sharp 'kinks' near 80% utilization.

cards.heading: real-world example
cards.body: You deposit 1,000 USDC into Aave on Base. The current supply APY is 6%, so you earn ~$60/year passively. Other users borrow that USDC at 8% APY, posting ETH as collateral. The 2% spread funds Aave's reserves. You can withdraw your USDC anytime, instantly.

cards.text: Unlike a bank, there's no credit check. Anyone with collateral can borrow instantly. The smart contract is the only intermediary, and rates adjust every second based on usage.
Key takeaway: DeFi lending replaces loan officers with smart contracts. Rates float with supply and demand, and everything happens in seconds.

cards.heading: why >100% collateral?
cards.body: In DeFi, there's no identity, credit score, or legal recourse. The only guarantee is your collateral. To protect lenders, protocols require you to deposit MORE value than you borrow — typically 120-150%. If your collateral drops, the protocol auto-sells it to repay the loan.

cards.heading: real-world example
cards.body: You want to borrow $1,000 USDC without selling your ETH. You deposit $1,500 of ETH as collateral on Aave (66% LTV). You walk away with $1,000 USDC to spend. As long as ETH stays above ~$1,200 worth, you're safe. Pay back the loan anytime to reclaim your ETH.

cards.text: Overcollateralization is why DeFi lending works without credit checks. The protocol can always sell your collateral to recover the loan — the math is the only protection.
Key takeaway: in DeFi you borrow against your assets, not your identity. The trade-off is you need MORE assets than you want to borrow.

cards.heading: the number that keeps you safe
cards.body: Health Factor = (Collateral Value × Liquidation Threshold) / Borrow Value. Above 1.0, you're safe. At exactly 1.0, you get liquidated. Most experienced users aim to stay above 1.5 for a comfortable buffer against price swings.

cards.heading: what happens at liquidation
cards.body: When HF drops to 1.0, anyone can become a 'liquidator' — they repay part of your debt and take your collateral at a 5-10% discount as their reward. You lose that collateral permanently and still owe the remaining debt minus what was repaid.

cards.heading: real-world example
cards.body: You deposit $10,000 of ETH (LT 82.5%) and borrow $5,000 USDC. HF = (10,000 × 0.825) / 5,000 = 1.65 — comfortable. If ETH drops 30% to $7,000, HF = (7,000 × 0.825) / 5,000 = 1.155 — getting risky. Another 7% drop and you're liquidated.

cards.text: A health factor of 1.1 means a 10% drop in your collateral's price could trigger liquidation. Volatile assets like memecoins as collateral are dangerous — set price alerts.
Key takeaway: HF is your safety dashboard. Stay above 1.5 to sleep at night. Watch it like you'd watch your bank balance.

cards.heading: two different numbers
cards.body: LTV (Loan-to-Value) is the maximum you can borrow against your collateral when you open a loan — e.g., 75% LTV means $750 max per $1,000 collateral. The Liquidation Threshold is HIGHER (e.g., 82.5%) — the point where the protocol actually liquidates you.

cards.heading: the buffer zone
cards.body: The gap between LTV (75%) and Liquidation Threshold (82.5%) is your safety buffer. If you borrow the maximum at 75%, you only have 7.5% of cushion before liquidation. Smart borrowers borrow at 50-60% of max LTV, giving themselves a 30%+ price drop tolerance.

cards.heading: real-world example
cards.body: Aave's ETH parameters on Base: LTV 80%, LT 82.5%. You deposit $10,000 ETH and borrow $8,000 (max LTV) of USDC. ETH only needs to drop 3.1% for you to be liquidated. Borrow $5,000 instead (50% of LTV), and ETH would need to drop 39% to liquidate you.

cards.text: Rule of thumb: borrow at 40-60% of max LTV. This gives you room to absorb a 25-40% price drop without getting liquidated. Crypto is volatile — buffer is everything.
Key takeaway: max LTV is the temptation, liquidation threshold is the cliff. The space between them is your survival zone.

cards.heading: variable rate
cards.body: Changes based on pool utilization — when demand is high, rates spike. Aave's ETH borrow rate has gone from 1% to 50%+ in volatile periods. Variable is good when you expect rates to stay low or you plan to repay quickly. Most DeFi borrowing uses variable rates.

cards.heading: stable rate
cards.body: Locks in a rate for predictability, but typically starts higher than the current variable rate. Some protocols (like Aave V3) offer this — though under extreme conditions, it can be rebalanced. Useful for long-term loans where you want predictable interest.

cards.heading: real-world example
cards.body: You're borrowing $10,000 USDC for 1 year. Variable rate is 5%, stable rate is 7%. If rates stay low, you save $200 with variable. If rates spike to 15% mid-year, variable could cost you $1,000+ extra. Stable rates are an insurance product — you pay a premium for certainty.

cards.text: Supply APY is almost always lower than Borrow APY — the spread funds the protocol's reserves and revenue. This is how lending protocols sustain themselves without venture capital.
Key takeaway: variable for short-term/low-rate environments, stable for long-term certainty. You're now ready to use the Health Factor Calculator and stress-test your positions!
